title: Value Is Income Divided by a Rate
summary: A finished income property is worth its net operating income divided by the market's capitalisation rate. A developer creates value by building that income for less than the market will pay for it. Yield on cost and the development spread tell you, before you buy land, whether that gap exists.
body:
An income property is worth the cash it throws off each year, divided by the rate the market demands for that cash. Your whole job as a developer is to create that income for less than the market will pay for it, and to know the size of the gap before you commit a dollar.

Recall

Q. In Phase 1 you set a personal liquidity floor. What is it, and why does it come before any deal?

A. It is the amount of cash you will not touch for any opportunity, however good it looks. It comes first because a developer who is forced to sell or borrow in a bad month loses far more than one deal.

Q. What does a power of attorney do that a will does not?

A. A power of attorney lets someone act for you while you are alive but unable to act. A will speaks only after death. A gap between the two leaves your affairs frozen if you are incapacitated.

Q. What is the outside view?

A. Judging a plan by how similar projects actually turned out, its reference class, before you look at the details that make yours feel special.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, every other number in this phase hangs off one equation. Lenders size loans from it. Buyers price buildings with it. Appraisers write it into their reports. Investors use it to decide whether your project is worth their money. If you cannot do this arithmetic in your head and explain it calmly, you will be negotiating with people who can, and they will set the terms. If you can, you will spot a bad deal on the first page of a broker's package, which is where most of the money in this business is saved.

Net operating income: the engine

Start with plain English. Net operating income is the money a property earns from running it, before you pay the bank and before income tax. Abbreviated, it is NOI.

The professional framing has three lines. First, potential gross income: every unit leased at market rent for twelve months. Second, subtract vacancy and credit loss, the rent you will not actually collect, to reach effective gross income. Third, subtract operating expenses: property tax, insurance, utilities the owner pays, repairs, management, payroll, and similar costs of running the building. What is left is NOI.

Notice what is not in there. Debt service is not in NOI, because NOI describes the building, not your loan. Depreciation is not in NOI, because it is an accounting entry, not cash. Income tax is not in NOI, because it depends on who owns the building. Major capital replacements are handled differently by different practitioners; some deduct a reserve for them, some do not. Always ask which convention a number uses.

Applied example, hypothetical round numbers. A 40-unit building has potential gross income of $1,050,000 a year. Vacancy and credit loss run 5 percent, about $50,000, leaving effective gross income of $1,000,000. Operating expenses are $400,000. NOI is $600,000.

The capitalisation rate: the price of a dollar of income

The capitalisation rate, or cap rate, is NOI divided by value. Turn it around and value equals NOI divided by the cap rate. If buyers of buildings like this one are paying prices that work out to a 6 percent cap rate, the building above is worth $600,000 divided by 0.06, which is $10,000,000.

The professional framing: a cap rate is not a return you earn. It is a market observation, the ratio buyers and sellers have recently accepted for a type of asset, in a type of location, at a point in the cycle. It bundles together interest rates, the risk of the income, and what buyers expect income to do in future. A low cap rate means buyers will pay a lot for each dollar of income, because they see it as safe or growing. A high cap rate means they will pay less.

Here is the property that makes cap rates dangerous. Because value is NOI divided by a small number, a small change in that number moves value a lot. At 6 percent, our building is worth $10,000,000. At 6.5 percent, it is worth about $9,230,000. Half a percentage point, which looks like a rounding error on a slide, has removed about $770,000 of value.

Say that out loud now. Value equals net operating income divided by the cap rate. Half a point on the cap rate can erase a year of income.

Yield on cost and the development spread

Now the developer's version. Yield on cost is the stabilised NOI divided by the total cost to create the project: land, hard costs, soft costs, financing costs and contingency. Stabilised means the building is leased up and running normally, not in its first chaotic months.

Suppose you can build the same 40 units for an all-in cost of $8,000,000. Your yield on cost is $600,000 divided by $8,000,000, or 7.5 percent. The market cap rate is 6 percent. The difference, 1.5 percentage points, is your development spread. Practitioners often say it in basis points, where 100 basis points is 1 percentage point, so this is a 150 basis point spread.

The spread is where development profit comes from. You spend $8,000,000 to create a building the market values at $10,000,000. The $2,000,000 difference is created value, 25 percent on cost. A tidy way to remember it: profit on cost equals yield on cost divided by cap rate, minus one. Here, 7.5 divided by 6 is 1.25, so 25 percent.

How big should the spread be? There is no standard. Many developers talk about wanting somewhere around 1 to 2 percentage points; treat that as commercial habit, not a rule, and it should widen as risk rises. The spread has to pay you for years of construction risk, lease-up risk, cost overruns and the chance that the cap rate rises before you finish. A thin spread on a risky project is not a deal; it is a donation.

How the best do it

Disciplined institutional investors tend to share three habits a small developer can copy. They underwrite the exit cap rate higher than today's cap rate, so their plan survives a softer market at completion. They separate in-place income from hoped-for income and price them differently. And they track construction cost inflation with published indices; Turner Construction, for example, publishes a quarterly building cost index for the United States. You can do all three on one sheet of paper.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is that your spread exists only on paper because your yield on cost uses a hopeful NOI while the market cap rate is today's. Rents slip, costs rise, cap rates widen, and a 150 basis point spread becomes zero. The control: build the spread from three cases, base, downside and severe, and decide in advance the minimum spread below which you walk away. Write it down before you see the land price, so the deal cannot talk you out of it.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner divides gross rent by the price and calls it a cap rate. Gross rent ignores vacancy and every operating expense, so it can overstate the true cap rate by a third or more. The second beginner's mistake is to subtract mortgage payments before calculating NOI. That mixes the building with your financing, and nobody on the other side of the table will accept the number.

Callback

In Week 2 you learned the outside view: judge a plan by how similar projects actually turned out. Apply it here. Before you trust your own yield on cost, ask what yield on cost comparable projects in your market really achieved once they were finished and leased, not what their brochures promised. That reference class is the honest check on your spread.

Recap

NOI is income from running the building, before debt and tax. Value is NOI divided by the cap rate, and small cap rate moves cause large value moves. Yield on cost is stabilised NOI divided by total project cost. The development spread, yield on cost minus the market cap rate, is the source of development profit, and it must be large enough to pay for the risk.

Next: Ford, with Roman assisting, on how the purchase of Stuyvesant Town failed on income that was never there.
checklist: Calculate NOI from effective gross income, never from gross rent.
Confirm NOI excludes debt service, depreciation and income tax.
Ask whether any quoted NOI deducts a capital reserve.
Write value as NOI divided by cap rate, and test it at plus half a point.
Compute yield on cost on the full all-in cost, including land and finance costs.
State the development spread in basis points.
Set a minimum acceptable spread before you see the land price.
Check yield on cost against what comparable finished projects actually achieved.
head: Field checklist
speak: Value in income property comes from one equation. Net operating income, the money a building earns from operating, before the mortgage and before income tax, divided by the capitalisation rate the market is paying for that kind of income. A 600,000 dollar NOI at a 6 percent cap rate is a 10 million dollar building. Because you divide by a small number, small changes in the cap rate move value a lot: half a point erases close to 800,000 dollars here. As a developer, I measure yield on cost, stabilised NOI divided by every dollar it takes to create the building. If I can build that 600,000 dollar income for 8 million, my yield on cost is 7.5 percent, and the 150 basis point gap over the market cap rate is my development spread. That spread is my profit and my safety margin. I set the minimum I will accept before I look at the land price.
terms: Net operating income (NOI) — the annual income from operating a property after vacancy and operating expenses, before debt service, depreciation and income tax.
Capitalisation rate — NOI divided by value; a market observation of what buyers pay for a dollar of income, not a return you earn.
Development spread — yield on cost minus the market cap rate, usually stated in basis points; the margin that pays for development risk.

hostile.q: Your yield on cost is 7.5 percent against a 6 percent cap rate today. What is the spread if cap rates are 6.75 percent when you finish, and why should I still invest?
hostile.a: At 6.75 percent the spread falls to 75 basis points and profit on cost falls from 25 percent to about 11 percent. I have tested that case. The project still covers its debt and returns capital in that downside, and my walk-away floor was set at 100 basis points before I saw the land price, so if today's numbers fell below it I would not be here. If you need a wider cushion, the lever is land price, and I will show you the land value at which the downside spread reaches your number.

title: Stuyvesant Town: Paying Today for Income That Never Came
summary: In 2006 a buyer paid a record price for a large Manhattan rental complex on the strength of income it planned to create later. Credit tightened, a court ruling closed the main route to that income, and the owners handed the property to lenders in 2010. The lesson is to price future income as a separate, survivable bet.
body:
Stuyvesant Town did not fail because the buildings were bad. It failed because the price paid in 2006 assumed net operating income that did not yet exist and that depended on things the buyer did not control.

Recall

Q. In the Phase 1 checkpoint you rehearsed acknowledge, bridge, answer. What is it for?

A. A hostile question. You acknowledge the concern, bridge to the relevant fact, and answer directly, without arguing or retreating.

Q. What is the purpose of an emergency reserve on a personal balance sheet?

A. To meet obligations through a bad stretch without selling assets or borrowing on poor terms. It buys time.

Q. What is a pre-mortem?

A. Before a decision, you imagine it has already failed and list the reasons why. It surfaces risks that optimism hides.

Why this matters

Ford here, with Roman alongside. Mr Shabazz, yesterday Sage gave you the equation: value is NOI divided by the cap rate. This case shows what happens when the NOI in that equation is a forecast dressed as a fact. It is one of the most widely reported real estate failures of its decade, and every step of it maps onto a decision you will make yourself.

Step 1: Timeline

Stuyvesant Town and the neighbouring Peter Cooper Village are a large post-war rental complex in Manhattan, built and long owned by the insurer MetLife. In 2006 MetLife sold the complex to a venture led by Tishman Speyer and BlackRock for a reported price of about 5.4 billion US dollars, then widely described as a record for a single American residential property. The purchase was financed mostly with debt, and reserves were set aside to help cover the gap between the income in place and the debt payments. Through 2007 and 2008 the credit crisis hit. In 2009 New York's highest court ruled in a case known as Roberts v. Tishman Speyer that apartments in buildings receiving a particular tax benefit could not be taken out of rent regulation in the way the owners had been doing. In January 2010 the owners defaulted and turned the property over to the lenders. The equity invested was reported to be lost.

Step 2: Key decisions

The decisive choice was the price. Measured against the income actually in place, the purchase price implied a very low cap rate. It only made sense if NOI rose substantially. The second choice was the capital structure: heavy debt, with reserves meant to bridge the years before income caught up. The third was the business plan: convert regulated apartments to market rents as tenants left.

Step 3: Assumptions

Three assumptions carried the deal. That regulated units could be moved to market rent at a steady pace. That market rents in Manhattan would keep rising. And that credit would remain available on similar terms if refinancing was needed. Each assumption was reasonable on its own. Together they made the whole price depend on several uncertain things happening at once.

Step 4: Incentives

Roman's angle. In a competitive auction, the winning bidder is often the one with the most optimistic forecast, which is called the winner's curse. Lenders and investors in that period were competing to deploy capital. Sellers wanted the highest price. Few people in the chain were paid to say the forecast was too hopeful. When everyone around a deal is rewarded for it closing, nobody is rewarded for stopping it.

Step 5: Warning signs ignored

The clearest sign was arithmetic. If a price only works after income rises a great deal, the price is a bet, not a valuation. A second sign was dependence on reserves: when a plan needs a cash reserve to pay the debt during the early years, the reserve is a countdown clock. A third was legal: the treatment of rent-regulated units was contested by tenants before the court ruled. Contested law is a risk to be priced, not ignored.

Say that out loud now. If the price only works after income rises, the price is a bet, not a valuation.

Step 6: Point of no return

The point of no return was the closing itself, at that price and with that much debt. After closing, the owners could only win if the forecast came true on time. When credit froze and then the court ruling arrived, there was no lever left: the income could not rise fast enough, the reserves were being consumed, and refinancing on acceptable terms was not available.

Step 7: Root cause

The root cause was capitalising future NOI as if it were in-place NOI, and financing that price with debt that needed the future to arrive on schedule. The tools in Sage's lesson were all there. The error was in what was fed into them.

The developer's version of this mistake

You will not buy a 5 billion dollar complex, but you can make the same error at any size. Hypothetical example: a small apartment building earns $300,000 of NOI today. The seller's broker shows a pro forma NOI of $420,000 after renovations and rent increases, and prices the building at a 6 percent cap rate on that future number: $7,000,000. On today's NOI, the same price is a 4.3 percent cap rate. If market buildings like it trade at 6 percent, today's income is worth $5,000,000. You would be paying $2,000,000 for income that does not exist yet, and you would also be paying for the renovation that creates it.

The disciplined approach separates the two. Value the in-place NOI at the market cap rate. Then treat the upside as a project: cost to renovate, time to re-lease, probability it works, and what happens if it does not. Pay only a share of the upside, and make sure your debt can be serviced from in-place income.

Roman adds the lender's arithmetic, again with hypothetical numbers. Suppose a lender wants yearly NOI to be at least 1.25 times the yearly loan payments; that multiple is commercial practice and varies by lender. On today's $300,000 of NOI, the most you can pay the bank each year is $240,000. On the broker's $420,000, it would be $336,000. A loan sized on the broker's number needs $96,000 a year that the building does not earn. Somebody has to write that cheque every year until the rents arrive, and that somebody is you, from reserves or from your own pocket. That is exactly the position the Stuyvesant Town owners were in at a far larger scale. Size the loan to the income you have. If the upside arrives, refinance then.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is that the forecast becomes the base case without anyone saying so. The control is a two-line valuation on every acquisition: line one, in-place NOI at the market cap rate; line two, the separately priced upside. If the loan cannot be carried by line one alone, you need more equity or a lower price.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner reads the broker's pro forma NOI as the property's NOI. A broker's projection is a marketing document. Ask for the trailing twelve months of actual income and expenses, the rent roll, and the leases, and build your own number.

Callback

In Week 2 you learned the pre-mortem. Run one on this deal as if it were 2006: imagine it is 2010 and the owners have handed back the keys. The likely causes appear in seconds: credit tightens, a legal route closes, the reserves run out. A pre-mortem would not have predicted the court ruling, but it would have asked what happens if the income plan stalls, and demanded an answer.

Recap

Stuyvesant Town was bought at a price that capitalised hoped-for income, financed with debt that needed that income on schedule. Credit tightened and a court ruling closed the main route to higher rents. Value in-place income and upside separately, and size debt to in-place income.

Rule 10: Price in-place income at the market cap rate, treat future income as a separately priced bet the deal can survive losing, and never borrow against income that does not yet exist.

Next: Roman on what a cap rate move does to your equity, not just to the building.
checklist: Ask for trailing twelve months of actual income and expenses, not a pro forma.
Value in-place NOI at the market cap rate as line one.
Price any upside separately, with its own cost, time and probability.
Confirm the debt can be serviced from in-place income alone.
Treat any reserve that funds debt service as a countdown clock.
List the legal and regulatory assumptions the income plan depends on.
Run a pre-mortem before signing a purchase agreement.
head: Field checklist
speak: In 2006 a venture bought Stuyvesant Town in Manhattan for a reported price of about 5.4 billion dollars. The price only made sense if net operating income rose a lot, by moving rent-regulated apartments to market rents. It was financed mostly with debt, with reserves to cover the early shortfall. Then credit froze, and in 2009 New York's highest court ruled that many of those apartments could not be deregulated the way the owners had been doing. In January 2010 the owners handed the property to the lenders. The root cause was capitalising future income as if it were in-place income, and borrowing against it. My rule: price in-place income at the market cap rate, treat future income as a separately priced bet the deal can survive losing, and never borrow against income that does not yet exist.
terms: Winner's curse — the tendency for the winning bidder in a competitive auction to be the one who most overestimated the asset's value.
In-place NOI — net operating income the property actually earns now under existing leases, as opposed to projected NOI.
Pro forma — a projected statement of future income and costs; a forecast, not a record.

hostile.q: Your offer values the building on today's income, well below the broker's number. Why should the seller take you seriously?
hostile.a: Because my offer is the price at which I can close with certainty. Today's NOI at the market cap rate is the value a lender will finance and an appraiser will support. I have priced part of the renovation upside on top of that, but I will not pay you for income I have to create, fund and risk myself. If the upside is as solid as the pro forma says, the seller can capture it by doing the work and selling later.

rule: Rule 10: Price in-place income at the market cap rate, treat future income as a separately priced bet the deal can survive losing, and never borrow against income that does not yet exist.

title: A Cap Rate Move Hits Your Equity First
summary: When cap rates rise, the building loses a percentage of its value, but your equity loses a much larger percentage because the loan does not shrink. Leverage magnifies cap rate moves in both directions. Mark your stake conservatively and know the cap rate at which your equity disappears.
body:
A cap rate move changes the value of the building by a few percent and the value of your equity by many times that, because the loan stays the same size while the value moves. Know the cap rate at which your equity is gone before you sign.

Recall

Q. In the Phase 1 mock meeting, what does "I'll confirm by Friday" protect you from?

A. Guessing under pressure. It commits you to a specific answer by a specific time instead of inventing a number in the room.

Q. In Week 8, why is insurance treated as part of protecting the base rather than as an investment?

A. Its job is to transfer a loss you could not absorb, so the rest of the plan survives a bad event. Its value is in the protection, not in a return.

Q. What is inversion, from Week 2?

A. Instead of asking how to succeed, you ask what would guarantee failure, and then avoid those things.

Why this matters

Roman here, risk and the lender's view. Mr Shabazz, Sage taught you that value is NOI divided by the cap rate. Ford showed you an owner losing a building. This lesson connects the two. Your wealth is not the building. Your wealth is the building minus the debt against it. That difference behaves very differently from the building itself, and lenders, partners and appraisers will all be watching it.

Leverage magnifies the move

Plain English first. Loan-to-value, or LTV, is the loan divided by the property's value. If you borrow $6,500,000 against a $10,000,000 building, your LTV is 65 percent and your equity, the owner's share of value, is $3,500,000.

Now let the cap rate rise. NOI stays at $600,000 throughout, hypothetical round numbers.

Cap rateBuilding valueLoanEquityChange in equity
6.0 percent$10,000,000$6,500,000$3,500,000none
6.5 percent$9,230,769$6,500,000$2,730,769down 22 percent
7.0 percent$8,571,429$6,500,000$2,071,429down 41 percent

The building lost about 8 percent of its value when the cap rate rose half a point. Your equity lost 22 percent. At a full point, the building is down about 14 percent and your equity is down 41 percent. That multiplier is leverage. It works upward too, which is why people borrow, but the downside arrives faster than most owners expect.

The professional framing is the break-even cap rate: the cap rate at which equity reaches zero. That is NOI divided by the loan. Here, $600,000 divided by $6,500,000 is about 9.2 percent. Below that, you still own something. Above it, the lender owns the economic value. Roman wants that number on the first page of every deal summary.

Say that out loud now. My equity is value minus debt, and the debt does not shrink when cap rates rise.

The race between income and the cap rate

Cap rate expansion means cap rates rising, which pushes values down. It is not the only force. If NOI grows at the same time, the two fight. Applied example: NOI grows 5 percent to $630,000 while the cap rate rises to 6.5 percent. Value is $630,000 divided by 0.065, about $9,690,000. Income growth recovered most of the loss, but not all of it. You need roughly 8 percent NOI growth just to stand still against a half-point cap rate rise from 6 percent.

This is why lenders also watch debt yield, NOI divided by the loan amount. It ignores the cap rate entirely and asks a blunt question: if the lender had to take the building, how much income would it earn on the money it lent? Here, $600,000 on $6,500,000 is 9.2 percent, the same number as the break-even cap rate, because it is the same arithmetic seen from the lender's side.

What this does to a development

For a developer the danger is timing. You commit to land and construction based on today's cap rate, and you sell or refinance at the cap rate prevailing two or three years later. Applied example: you build for $8,000,000, expecting $600,000 of stabilised NOI and a 6 percent exit cap rate, a value of $10,000,000. Your construction loan is $5,600,000, so your equity is $2,400,000. If the exit cap rate is 7 percent, value is about $8,570,000. After repaying the loan, equity is about $2,970,000. You made money, but your expected profit of $2,000,000 shrank to about $570,000, a fall of more than 70 percent on a one-point cap rate move. Your margin for error was your spread, and most of it was consumed.

The refinancing gap

Here is where cap rates turn into a cheque you must write. Suppose the $6,500,000 loan from the first table matures in five years, and the lender who refinances it will lend 65 percent of value. That percentage is commercial practice and varies by lender and asset. If cap rates are still 6 percent, the new loan is $6,500,000 and you simply roll it over. If cap rates have risen to 7 percent and NOI has not grown, value is about $8,571,000 and the new loan is 65 percent of that, about $5,571,000. You owe $6,500,000. The difference, about $929,000, must come from somewhere: your cash, a new partner, a more expensive second loan, or a sale at a bad moment. Nothing went wrong with the building. The tenants paid. The only thing that changed was the market's price for income. That is the mechanism behind most of the maturity crises you will study in later post-mortems, and it is why Roman reads the maturity date before the interest rate.

Wealth Ledger

Warrick here. On your personal balance sheet, a stake in a building is not worth what the last appraisal said. It is an estimate that depends on a cap rate you do not control. Three habits follow. Record your equity at a conservative cap rate, at least half a point above today's, so a market move does not shock you. Never count unsold development profit as wealth; it is a forecast until a sale or refinance turns it into cash. And watch concentration: if one leveraged building is most of your net worth, a one-point cap rate move can take a third or more of everything you own. Concentration is how developers build wealth and how they lose it. A licensed adviser is required before you act on any personal allocation.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is borrowing to the limit at a low cap rate, at the top of a cycle, with a short loan term. If the loan matures when cap rates have risen, the new loan will be sized on a lower value, and you must find fresh equity to repay the difference. The control: know your break-even cap rate, keep LTV low enough that a one-point rise does not trigger a refinancing gap, and match loan maturity to a time you can afford to wait.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner reads a fall in building value as a fall in personal wealth of the same percentage. It is always larger with debt. The second mistake is assuming rent growth will cover cap rate expansion. It sometimes does, slowly. Cap rates can move in a single year.

Callback

In Week 2 you learned inversion. Apply it here: instead of asking what return you will make, ask what cap rate would wipe out your equity, and how likely the market is to reach it before your loan matures. That single inverted question, answered with the break-even cap rate, is worth more than any upside slide.

Recap

Equity is value minus debt, and leverage magnifies every cap rate move. Know the break-even cap rate, which is NOI divided by the loan. Income growth can offset cap rate expansion, but slowly. On your personal balance sheet, mark stakes conservatively and treat unsold profit as a forecast.

Next: Vera on the rules that govern an appraisal, and how to read one.
checklist: Calculate LTV on every deal and every refinance.
Compute the break-even cap rate: NOI divided by the loan.
Show equity at today's cap rate, plus half a point and plus one point.
Calculate the NOI growth needed to offset a half-point cap rate rise.
Match the loan maturity to a window you can afford to wait through.
Record personal stakes at a conservative cap rate.
Never count unsold development profit as personal wealth.
head: Field checklist
speak: My wealth in a building is its value minus its debt. When cap rates rise, the building loses a few percent and my equity loses many times that, because the loan does not shrink. On a 10 million dollar building with a 6.5 million dollar loan, a half-point rise in the cap rate takes about 8 percent off the building and 22 percent off my equity. A full point takes 41 percent. So I calculate the break-even cap rate, net operating income divided by the loan; that is the cap rate where my equity hits zero. Rent growth can fight back, but I would need about 8 percent NOI growth just to offset a half-point move. On my personal balance sheet, I record my stake at a cap rate above today's, I never count unsold profit as wealth, and I watch concentration, because one leveraged building can be most of what I own.
terms: Loan-to-value (LTV) — the loan amount divided by the property's value, expressed as a percentage.
Cap rate expansion — a rise in market cap rates, which lowers the value of each dollar of NOI.
Debt yield — NOI divided by the loan amount; the income a lender would earn on its money if it took the property.

hostile.q: Your exit assumes the same cap rate as today. What happens to my equity if rates are a point higher when you sell?
hostile.a: At one point higher, value falls about 14 percent and the profit I projected falls by more than 70 percent, but the loan is still fully repaid and your capital comes back with a modest gain. My break-even cap rate on the construction loan is above 10 percent, so equity is not wiped out in any case I consider plausible. I will send you the full sensitivity table by Friday, at plus a half, plus one and plus one and a half points.

title: The Appraisal Is a Document With Rules
summary: An appraisal is a professional opinion written for a named client and use, under published standards, with assumptions you must read. As-is and as-complete values answer different questions. Learn to read the assumptions and conditions before you read the number.
body:
An appraisal is not a price tag. It is a professional opinion of value, written for a stated client and a stated use, as of a stated date, under published standards and with assumptions that can change the answer completely. Read those before you read the number.

Recall

Q. In the Phase 1 checkpoint you were asked to record a three-minute explanation and score it. What were the four scores?

A. Accuracy, structure, composure and handling the hard question, each from 1 to 5.

Q. In Week 8, what is the difference between an emergency reserve and an investment?

A. A reserve is held for availability, so it sits in something you can reach quickly without loss. An investment is held for return and may not be available when you need it.

Q. What is an after-action review?

A. A short, structured look back after an event: what was supposed to happen, what happened, why, and what to do differently next time.

Why this matters

Vera here, records and evidence. Mr Shabazz, the cap rate equation becomes a legal and commercial document the moment an appraiser signs it. Your lender will size the loan on it. Your investors may rely on it. If it is wrong, misread or built on an assumption nobody noticed, the consequences land on you. You do not need to become an appraiser. You need to know what an appraisal is allowed to say, and how to read what it actually says.

The standards behind the report

In plain English, appraisers in most developed markets follow a written code of practice. In the United States, the main one is the Uniform Standards of Professional Appraisal Practice, known as USPAP, issued by the Appraisal Standards Board of The Appraisal Foundation. In Canada, members of the Appraisal Institute of Canada follow the Canadian Uniform Standards of Professional Appraisal Practice, known as CUSPAP. Internationally there are the International Valuation Standards, and many surveyors follow the Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors' global standards, known as the Red Book. These documents are revised periodically; verify the current edition and which one applies in your market against the primary source before you rely on it.

The professional framing is that these standards govern how an appraiser works, not what number they reach. They require the appraiser to be impartial, to identify the problem being solved, to disclose assumptions, and to keep a work file supporting the conclusion. Licensing and certification are separate, set by the jurisdiction where the property sits. Professional sign-off required: a designated or certified appraiser licensed for that jurisdiction and property type.

Five things every report must tell you

Read these before the value. First, the client and intended user: who ordered the report and who may rely on it. If a lender ordered it, you usually cannot rely on it yourself unless the appraiser agrees in writing, often through a reliance letter. Second, the intended use: financing, purchase, litigation, insurance. A value for one use is not automatically valid for another. Third, the definition of value, usually market value, which the report will define in words. Fourth, the effective date: the date the value applies to, which is not the date the report was written. Fifth, the property rights appraised: full ownership, a leasehold, or something else.

Applied example. A report states a market value of $10,000,000, effective as of a date eight months ago, ordered by a lender for financing. For your purposes today it is eight months stale, written for someone else, and possibly not one you are entitled to rely on. The number may still be right. But you cannot treat it as evidence for a new decision without fresh work.

Say that out loud now. Client, use, definition, date, rights. I read those before I read the value.

As-is, as-complete and as-stabilised

For development, the most important distinction is which point in time the value describes. An as-is value describes the property today, perhaps a vacant lot or a half-built shell. An as-complete value is a prospective opinion of what the finished building will be worth when construction is done. An as-stabilised value describes the finished building once it is leased up and operating normally.

Applied example, hypothetical. Your land is worth $1,500,000 as-is. The finished building is appraised at $9,000,000 as-complete and $10,000,000 as-stabilised. A construction lender lending 65 percent of the as-stabilised value would lend $6,500,000. One lending 65 percent of as-complete would lend $5,850,000. The $650,000 difference is equity you must find. Always ask which value a loan offer is sized on.

Assumptions that change everything

USPAP uses two terms you must recognise. An extraordinary assumption is something the appraiser assumes to be true, as of the effective date, that is uncertain and would change the result if false; for example, that a zoning approval will be granted. A hypothetical condition is something the appraiser knows is not true but assumes for the purpose of the analysis; for example, that a building which does not yet exist is complete. A prospective as-complete value usually rests on assumptions like these. They are legitimate when disclosed. They are dangerous when you skim past them.

Your control is simple. Before accepting any value, list every extraordinary assumption and hypothetical condition in the report, and ask of each: is it true, is it likely, and what is the value if it is wrong? If the value depends on an approval you do not yet have, that dependency belongs in your risk register.

Applied example, hypothetical. An as-complete value of $9,000,000 is stated on the extraordinary assumption that a rezoning permitting 40 units will be approved. If the approval is refused and the site can only take 30 units, NOI falls by roughly a quarter and so does value: something near $6,750,000, before any change in cost per unit. A loan sized on $9,000,000 would now exceed what the project can support, and the gap would arrive at the worst possible moment, after the land is bought and design money is spent. The assumption was disclosed on page 14. The borrower who read only page 1 learned about it from the lender. That is the whole difference between reading a report and owning its conclusion.

Independence

Appraisal standards require impartiality, and many lending systems add rules about who may order an appraisal and who may communicate with the appraiser. The details differ by jurisdiction and lender; verify them against the primary source before you rely on them. The practical rule is universal: you may supply facts, documents and comparable sales, and you may point out errors. You must never ask for, hint at or reward a particular number.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is treating a prospective value as a present fact. An as-stabilised value assumes construction finishes, leases sign and the market holds. The control: record the value type, effective date and every assumption in your decision log beside the number, and size your commitments to the as-is position plus what you can survive losing.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner turns to the last page, finds the number, and stops reading. The limiting conditions, assumptions and scope of work are where the report tells you what the number does not mean.

Callback

Ford's Rule 10 told you to price in-place income separately from future income. An appraisal makes that split explicit: as-is value is the in-place view, as-stabilised value is the future view. When the two are far apart, the gap is the bet you are making, and the extraordinary assumptions tell you what has to go right.

Recap

Appraisals follow published standards such as USPAP and CUSPAP. Read client, intended use, definition of value, effective date and property rights first. Distinguish as-is, as-complete and as-stabilised. List every extraordinary assumption and hypothetical condition. Never influence the number.

Next: Sage, working backward from a finished building to the most you can pay for land.
checklist: Identify the client and intended user of the report.
Confirm whether you may rely on it, and obtain a reliance letter if needed.
Note the definition of value and the effective date.
Record whether the value is as-is, as-complete or as-stabilised.
List every extraordinary assumption and hypothetical condition.
Ask which value any loan offer is sized on.
Confirm the appraiser is designated or certified for that jurisdiction and property type.
Supply facts and corrections only; never suggest a number.
head: Field checklist
speak: An appraisal is a professional opinion of value, not a price tag. It follows published standards, USPAP in the United States and CUSPAP for Canadian designated appraisers, and it is written for a named client and use, as of an effective date. Before I read the number, I read five things: who the client is, the intended use, the definition of value, the effective date and the property rights appraised. For development, I check which value I am looking at. As-is is today. As-complete is the finished building. As-stabilised is the building leased up and running. Lenders size loans on one of those, and the difference can be hundreds of thousands of dollars of equity. Then I list every extraordinary assumption and hypothetical condition, because a prospective value rests on them. I may give an appraiser facts. I never ask for a number.
terms: Intended use and intended user — the purpose an appraisal was prepared for and the parties entitled to rely on it.
Extraordinary assumption — an uncertain fact assumed true as of the effective date which, if false, could change the appraiser's conclusion.
Hypothetical condition — a condition known to be contrary to fact, such as a finished building that does not yet exist, assumed for the purpose of the analysis.

hostile.q: Your appraisal shows 10 million as-stabilised. Why should our credit committee lend against anything above the as-is value?
hostile.a: You should not lend on as-stabilised value alone, and I am not asking you to. The as-stabilised figure rests on disclosed assumptions: completion, lease-up and today's market. I have listed each one, with its status and the value if it fails. I am asking you to size against the as-complete value with the construction risk covered by my equity, my contingency and the completion guarantee we will negotiate. Tell me which assumption worries your committee most and I will bring the evidence on it.

title: Working Backward From the Finished Building
summary: Start from what the market will pay for the finished, stabilised building, set the spread you need, and work backward to the maximum total cost and the most you can pay for land. Then reverse the question: what rent would a seller's asking price require?
body:
Do not start a deal with the land price. Start with what the market will pay for the finished building, decide the spread you need, and work backward to the most you can afford to spend. The land is whatever is left.

Recall

Q. What is the formula for value from income?

A. Value equals net operating income divided by the capitalisation rate.

Q. In Week 8 you sized an emergency reserve. What is it measured in?

A. Months of essential obligations it can cover, not a round dollar figure chosen for comfort.

Q. What is a reference class?

A. A group of similar past projects whose actual outcomes you use as the starting estimate for your own.

Why this matters

Sage here. Mr Shabazz, most people value land by asking what the seller wants and whether it feels reasonable. That lets the seller set the anchor, and you learned in Week 3 how strongly an anchor pulls. A developer reverses the order. The finished building's value is set by the market; your required profit is set by your own rules; construction costs are set by the market for labour and materials. The land is the only number left to solve for, so it is the number you solve for. This is called the residual method, because the land value is what remains.

Step 1: The finished outcome

All numbers are hypothetical. A 40-unit apartment building, once leased and stabilised, will earn net operating income of $600,000 a year. Comparable stabilised buildings in the area trade at about a 6 percent cap rate. So the finished building is worth $600,000 divided by 0.06, which is $10,000,000.

Step 2: The spread you require

You have decided, before looking at this site, that you need at least 150 basis points of development spread for this type and size of project. So your required yield on cost is 6 percent plus 1.5 percent, which is 7.5 percent.

Step 3: Maximum total cost

Yield on cost is NOI divided by total cost. Rearranged, the most you can spend is NOI divided by the required yield on cost: $600,000 divided by 0.075, which is $8,000,000. That is your all-in budget for everything: land, construction, fees, financing and contingency. Spend a dollar more and your spread falls below your floor.

Say that out loud now. Maximum total cost equals NOI divided by my required yield on cost.

Step 4: Subtract everything except land

Now take away every cost that is not land, using your best current estimates.

ItemBasisAmount
Hard costs40 units at $125,000 each$5,000,000
Soft costs20 percent of hard costs$1,000,000
Contingency5 percent of hard plus soft$300,000
Finance costsestimated interest and fees$600,000
Total, excluding land$6,900,000

The percentages for soft costs and contingency are illustrations, not standards; real figures come from your consultants and your estimate class, which Week 13 covers.

Step 5: The residual land value

Maximum total cost of $8,000,000, minus $6,900,000, leaves $1,100,000. That is the most you can pay for the land and still keep a 150 basis point spread. Per unit, it is $27,500. Units, always: say "per unit" or "per buildable square foot", because a land price on its own tells a listener nothing.

One honest refinement. Finance costs partly depend on the land price, because you borrow to buy land and pay interest on it through construction. If you pay more for land, interest rises too. For a first pass the error is small, but in a full pro forma the two are solved together.

Step 6: Check the answer against the market

A residual is only as good as its inputs, so test it against evidence. Gather recent land sales for similar sites, converted to the same unit, price per permitted apartment or per buildable square foot. Suppose, hypothetically, that comparable sites have sold for between $30,000 and $38,000 per unit, while your residual says $27,500. That gap is information, not an insult to your spreadsheet.

There are only a few possible explanations. The buyers of those sites may expect higher rents than you do, may build more cheaply, may accept a thinner spread, or may have overpaid. Each one is checkable. Look at what rents finished competing buildings are actually achieving. Ask a cost consultant whether $125,000 per unit is high for this product. Ask brokers what spreads recent buyers underwrote. If after that your inputs still stand, your residual stands, and the market for land is running ahead of the market for finished buildings. That is often a late-cycle signal, and Remi will return to it in Phase 4. If the evidence shows your inputs were too cautious, change them, record why, and rerun. Never change an input simply because the answer felt low.

Reverse engineering the seller's price

Now the seller asks $1,500,000. Do not argue. Calculate what the asking price requires to be true.

At $1,500,000 for land, total cost is $8,400,000. At the market rents you assumed, NOI is still $600,000, so yield on cost is $600,000 divided by $8,400,000, which is about 7.14 percent. Your spread is about 114 basis points, below your floor.

To restore a 7.5 percent yield on cost at that price, NOI would need to be $8,400,000 times 0.075, which is $630,000. Work that back to rent. Assume operating expenses of $400,000 a year, about $10,000 per unit. Effective gross income would need to be $630,000 plus $400,000, which is $1,030,000. With 5 percent vacancy, potential gross income must be $1,030,000 divided by 0.95, about $1,084,000. Across 40 units and 12 months, that is about $2,259 per unit per month.

Compare it with the rent behind your base case: $600,000 of NOI needs about $1,052,600 of potential income, or about $2,193 per unit per month. The seller's price therefore requires rents about $66 a month, or roughly 3 percent, above what the market supports today. Now you have a conversation instead of an argument: either the market rent evidence supports 3 percent more, or the land is overpriced by about $400,000.

The sensitivity that matters most

Run one more line: what if the exit cap rate is 6.5 percent instead of 6 percent? Keep the 150 basis point spread and the required yield on cost becomes 8 percent. Maximum total cost becomes $600,000 divided by 0.08, which is $7,500,000, and residual land value falls to $600,000. Half a point on the cap rate cut the land you can afford by almost half. That is why land is the most leveraged number in a development pro forma.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is solving backward from a target return and then adjusting the inputs until the land price fits. That is not reverse engineering; it is rationalising. The control: fix rent evidence, cost estimates, cap rate and required spread first, with sources noted beside each, and let the land value be whatever falls out.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner leaves out finance costs and contingency, and so overstates the land they can afford by hundreds of thousands of dollars. In this example, leaving out those two lines would have suggested $2,000,000 of land value instead of $1,100,000.

Callback

In Week 3 you studied anchoring: the first number in a conversation pulls every later number toward it. Residual land value is your defence. When you have calculated $1,100,000 before you hear the seller's $1,500,000, the seller's number is no longer an anchor. It is a claim, and you know exactly what has to be true for it to hold.

Recap

Start from the stabilised value, set the spread, divide NOI by the required yield on cost to get maximum total cost, subtract every non-land cost, and what remains is the residual land value. Then test any asking price by calculating the rent it would require.

Next: JAX in the room with an equity partner who does not believe your exit cap rate.
checklist: Start from stabilised NOI and the market cap rate.
Fix the required spread before looking at the site.
Compute maximum total cost: NOI divided by required yield on cost.
Subtract hard, soft, contingency and finance costs.
State residual land value per unit or per buildable square foot.
For any asking price, calculate the rent it requires.
Rerun the residual at a cap rate half a point higher.
Note the source beside every input.
head: Field checklist
speak: I never start with the land price. I start with the finished building. If it will earn 600,000 dollars of net operating income and similar buildings trade at a 6 percent cap rate, it is worth 10 million. I need a 150 basis point spread, so my yield on cost must be 7.5 percent. That makes my maximum total cost 600,000 divided by 0.075, which is 8 million. I subtract hard costs, soft costs, contingency and finance costs, 6.9 million in this case, and the residual, 1.1 million, is the most I can pay for land. If the seller wants 1.5 million, I do not argue. I calculate that his price needs rents about 3 percent above today's market. Either the evidence supports that, or the land is overpriced. And I always rerun it at a cap rate half a point higher, because that alone nearly halves the land value.
terms: Residual land value — the maximum price for land, found by subtracting every non-land cost and the required profit from the value of the finished project.
Required yield on cost — the market cap rate plus the development spread you demand; the hurdle total cost must meet.
Maximum total cost — stabilised NOI divided by required yield on cost; the all-in budget the project can bear.

hostile.q: Your residual says the land is worth 1.1 million. Three other developers are bidding 1.5. Why are you right and they are wrong?
hostile.a: I may not be right about their business plans. They may have cheaper construction, a lower required spread, or rent evidence I have not seen, and I would like to see it. What I know is that at 1.5 million, with the costs and rents I can evidence, my spread falls to about 114 basis points, below the floor I set before I saw this site. I would rather lose this land than buy a project that only works if rents beat today's market by 3 percent.

title: Defending Your Exit Cap Rate to a Sceptical Partner
summary: A prospective equity partner will attack the exit cap rate, because it moves value more than any other assumption. Answer with the range you tested, the evidence behind it and the case where the deal still works. Never defend a single number as if it were certain.
body:
The first serious question an equity partner asks about a development is usually about the exit cap rate, because it moves value more than anything else. Do not defend one number. Show the range you tested, where your evidence comes from, and the case in which the deal still works.

Recall

Q. What was Rule 10?

A. Price in-place income at the market cap rate, treat future income as a separately priced bet the deal can survive losing, and never borrow against income that does not yet exist.

Q. In Week 8, what does it mean to protect the base before taking risk?

A. Put the documents, insurance and reserves in place that keep your household and affairs functioning if something goes wrong, before you commit capital to anything risky.

Q. What is a decision journal?

A. A written record, made at the time, of a decision, the reasons, the expected outcome and how confident you were, so you can later judge the process rather than the luck.

Why this matters

JAX here, deals, partners and investors. Mr Shabazz, an equity partner is deciding two things in the first meeting: whether your numbers are right, and whether you can be trusted when they turn out wrong. The exit cap rate is where both questions meet. Handle it well and you earn the rest of the meeting. Handle it badly and nothing else on your slides gets read.

The scene

This is a composite example. You are presenting a hypothetical 40-unit project to the principal of a private investment firm considering a large share of the equity. Your summary shows total cost of $8,000,000, stabilised NOI of $600,000 and an exit value of $10,000,000 at a 6 percent cap rate. She has read it before the meeting. After two minutes of pleasantries she puts the page down.

"Six percent is today's number. You are finishing in three years. Why should I believe six?"

The question behind the question

She is not really asking for a forecast of cap rates. Nobody can give one, and she knows it. She is asking three things. Do you know how sensitive this deal is to the exit? Have you tested a bad case honestly? And will you tell her the truth when it is uncomfortable? Answer those three and the specific number matters much less.

The lines to say

Acknowledge, bridge, answer, the pattern from Week 6.

"You're right that six is today's number, and it's the assumption that moves value most. So I didn't rely on it. I tested six, six and a half, seven and seven and a half. At seven, profit falls from about 2 million to about 570 thousand, the construction loan is still repaid in full, and your capital comes back with a modest gain. At seven and a half the profit is gone and we roughly return capital. My land price was set so the seven case still works."

Then stop. Let her read the table. You have told her the sensitivity, the bad case, and the decision you made because of it.

If she pushes on the evidence: "My six comes from recent trades of stabilised buildings of this type in this submarket; the sale list is on page 4, with dates. I've weighted the most recent. If you have a trade I've missed, I want to see it."

If she asks something you cannot answer: "I don't know that yet. I'll confirm by Friday." Then confirm by Friday.

Say that out loud now. I didn't rely on six. I tested the range, and I priced the land so the bad case still works.

The lines never to say

"Cap rates will come down by then." You cannot know that, and saying it tells her your plan depends on it.

"The appraiser agreed with six." An appraisal states value at its effective date under its assumptions; it does not predict the future, and Vera showed you why.

"Everyone is using six." That is herd evidence. It is exactly what she is paid to distrust.

"Worst case, we just hold it." Holding costs money, needs a refinance, and may need fresh equity. Never offer a worst case you have not costed.

When to stay silent

After you show the downside table, stop talking. The urge to fill silence with reassurance is strong, and reassurance after a bad number sounds like doubt. Silence while she reads sounds like confidence in your homework. The same applies after she states her own view. If she says, "I'd underwrite seven," do not argue immediately. Ask, "What's driving seven for you?" Her answer tells you how she thinks, and that is worth more than winning the point.

Holding your state

Your heart rate will rise when she puts the page down. That is normal and, as Week 4 showed, you can treat that arousal as readiness rather than a threat. Take one slow breath out before your first word, keep your voice at your normal pace, and drop your pitch slightly at the end of statements rather than rising as if asking permission. Look at the numbers with her, not at her face for approval. A partner wants a developer who is calm about bad news, because there will be bad news.

The second worked example: her counter

Suppose she says, "I'll come in, but at a seven percent exit." Do the arithmetic aloud with her. At 7 percent the finished building is worth about $8,571,000. Your total cost is $8,000,000, so the profit is about $571,000, roughly 7 percent on cost. To restore a 25 percent profit on cost at a 7 percent exit, total cost would need to be about $6,857,000, which means about $1,143,000 less, and since construction costs are fixed by the market, that reduction has to come almost entirely out of the land. That tells both of you the real negotiation is the land price, not the cap rate. Say so: "Then the question isn't the cap rate. It's whether we can buy this land for about a million dollars less. I don't think we can. So at your number, this isn't our deal." Walking away calmly, with arithmetic, is how you earn the next deal.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is defending a single assumption so hard that your partner concludes you cannot see risk. The control: always present the cap rate as a range with a decision attached, and bring the downside table to every meeting, even when nobody asks for it.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner treats a challenge as an attack and responds with enthusiasm. Enthusiasm is not evidence. The beginner also concedes too fast: changing the exit to seven in the meeting to please the partner, without recalculating what that does to the deal.

Callback

Ford's case on Stuyvesant Town turned on income nobody would admit was a forecast. In this room you do the opposite. You name your forecast as a forecast, show what happens if it is wrong, and point to the decision you made because of it. That is Rule 10 spoken aloud.

Ethics thread: valuation integrity

Every number in this room is a temptation. You will be tempted to choose the comparable sale that flatters your cap rate, to leave the bad case off the slide, or to suggest to an appraiser that a particular value would help the loan. Each is a small act of misrepresentation, and in many systems pressuring an appraiser or misstating facts to a lender or investor carries legal consequences; verify the specific rules where you operate against the primary source.

The practical test is simple. Would you be comfortable if the other side saw every comparable you discarded and every message you sent the appraiser? If not, do not discard it and do not send it. Your reputation for honest numbers is the only asset in this business that compounds without leverage.

Recap

Expect the exit cap rate question first. Answer with the range, the evidence and the case where the deal still works. Stay silent while they read. If their number breaks the deal, say so with arithmetic and walk calmly.

Next: Kema, with six questions, a Red Pen drill and a two-minute boardroom explanation of value.
checklist: Bring a cap rate sensitivity table to every meeting.
Know profit and equity at plus a half, one and one and a half points.
List the comparable trades behind your cap rate, with dates.
Acknowledge, bridge, answer; then stop talking.
Ask what drives the other side's number before arguing.
Recalculate aloud before conceding any assumption.
Never suggest a value to an appraiser.
head: Field checklist
speak: When a partner challenges my exit cap rate, I don't defend one number. I say: you're right, six is today's number and it moves value more than anything else, so I tested six, six and a half, seven and seven and a half. At seven, profit falls from about 2 million to about 570 thousand, the loan is repaid and your capital comes back with a modest gain. I set the land price so that case still works. Then I stop and let her read. If she says she would underwrite seven, I ask what drives that, and I do the arithmetic aloud. If her number means the land must cost a million dollars less, I say the real question is the land, and if we can't get it, this isn't our deal. I never say cap rates will fall, and I never ask an appraiser for a number.
terms: Exit cap rate — the cap rate assumed when the finished building is sold or refinanced, usually years after the decision to build.
Sensitivity table — a grid showing how profit, value or equity change as one or two key assumptions vary.
Herd evidence — support for an assumption that rests on others using it rather than on transactions or data.

hostile.q: If cap rates go to seven and a half percent, I get my money back and nothing else after three years of risk. Why would I take that?
hostile.a: You should not take it as a base case, and I am not offering it as one. Seven and a half is my severe case: the return of capital, not a profit. I show it because you deserve to see where the floor is. The base case is a 25 percent profit on cost at six. The question for you is how likely seven and a half is by completion, compared with the return you are being paid for. If you think it is likely, the honest answer is a lower land price, and I will tell you whether I can get it.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 10 Review: Value, Spread and the Red Pen
summary: Six questions on NOI, cap rates, yield on cost and the development spread, a Red Pen drill on a flawed one-page valuation memo, and a two-minute boardroom explanation of how a developer creates value.
body:
This week came down to one idea: value is income divided by a rate, and a developer creates value only when the income costs less to build than the market will pay for it. Today you test that idea, find the errors in a flawed memo, and explain it in two minutes.

Recall

Q. What is the break-even cap rate?

A. NOI divided by the loan amount. It is the cap rate at which the owner's equity reaches zero.

Q. Week 8 closed with a review of protecting the base. Name two of its pieces.

A. A will and powers of attorney, adequate insurance, and an emergency reserve held for availability rather than return.

Q. Week 2 closed with judgment tools. What does an OODA loop stand for?

A. Observe, orient, decide, act: a cycle for making decisions faster and more accurately than the situation changes.

Why this matters

Kema here. Mr Shabazz, the numbers this week are the vocabulary of every lender, appraiser and investor you will meet. A review is not repetition for its own sake. It is the moment when ideas you understood on separate days become one tool you can use under pressure.

The six questions

Question 1. What is excluded from net operating income, and why? Answer: Debt service, depreciation and income tax. NOI describes the building's operations, not the owner's financing, accounting or tax position. Capital reserves are deducted by some practitioners and not others, so always ask.

Question 2. A building earns $450,000 of NOI and similar buildings trade at a 6 percent cap rate. What is it worth? Answer: $450,000 divided by 0.06 is $7,500,000.

Question 3. You can build that same income for $6,000,000. What are your yield on cost and spread? Answer: $450,000 divided by $6,000,000 is 7.5 percent. Minus the 6 percent cap rate, the spread is 150 basis points, and profit on cost is 25 percent.

Question 4. With a $4,500,000 loan on that $7,500,000 building, what happens to equity if the cap rate rises to 7 percent? Answer: Value falls to about $6,429,000. Equity falls from $3,000,000 to about $1,929,000, a drop of about 36 percent, against a 14 percent fall in the building.

Question 5. What is the difference between an as-is and an as-stabilised value? Answer: As-is describes the property today. As-stabilised is a prospective opinion of the finished building once it is leased and operating normally, and it rests on assumptions that must be read.

Question 6. What does Rule 10 say? Answer: Price in-place income at the market cap rate, treat future income as a separately priced bet the deal can survive losing, and never borrow against income that does not yet exist.

Say that out loud now. Value equals NOI over cap rate. Yield on cost equals NOI over total cost. The spread pays for the risk.

Speed round

Do these in your head, aloud, before checking. $300,000 of NOI at a 5 percent cap rate: $6,000,000. The same NOI at 6 percent: $5,000,000, a sixth less value for one point. A project costing $4,000,000 that earns $300,000: yield on cost 7.5 percent. Against a 6 percent market, profit on cost is 7.5 divided by 6, minus one: 25 percent. A $3,000,000 loan on that $5,000,000 building: break-even cap rate is $300,000 divided by $3,000,000, which is 10 percent. Finally, an equity partner offers terms that assume a 6.5 percent exit. Your required spread is 150 basis points, so your required yield on cost is 8 percent, and your maximum total cost on $300,000 of NOI is $3,750,000.

If any of those took you more than ten seconds, that is the one to practise this week. Speed is not the goal for its own sake. Speed frees your attention in the room for the person across the table, which is where deals are actually won or lost.

Recap of the week

Sage gave you the equation and the development spread. Ford showed Stuyvesant Town, where a price capitalised income that did not exist. Roman showed that leverage turns a small cap rate move into a large equity move. Vera taught you to read an appraisal's client, use, date and assumptions before its number. Sage worked backward from a finished building to residual land value. JAX put you in a room defending the exit cap rate with a range instead of a promise.

Red Pen drill

Read this hypothetical memo slowly. It contains six planted defects. Find them before reading on.

Project summary. 40 units. Gross rent $1,050,000 a year. NOI, after mortgage payments of $350,000 and depreciation of $150,000, is $550,000. Cap rate is gross rent divided by price. Total project cost $7,200,000, excluding land and financing. Yield on cost 7.6 percent. Market cap rate today 6 percent; we assume 5.5 percent at exit because the area is improving. Spread 210 basis points. As-complete appraisal received, value $10,000,000.

The defects. One: NOI has mortgage payments deducted; debt service never belongs in NOI. Two: depreciation is deducted; it is not cash and not part of NOI. Three: vacancy and operating expenses are nowhere in the calculation. Four: the cap rate is defined on gross rent, which overstates it. Five: total cost excludes land and financing, so yield on cost is overstated and the spread is inflated. Six: the exit cap rate is assumed lower than today's, with a reason that is a hope, not evidence, and the spread is then measured against that hopeful exit rate instead of today's market rate. A bonus defect for the careful reader: the appraisal is quoted with no effective date, no client and no assumptions, so nobody can tell what the $10,000,000 means.

Boardroom drill

Explain how a developer creates value in two minutes, as if to a board that knows business but not real estate. Then compare with this model answer.

"A finished rental building is valued by its net operating income, the cash it earns from operations before the mortgage and tax, divided by a capitalisation rate, the price the market pays per dollar of income. If buildings like ours trade at 6 percent, $600,000 of NOI is worth $10 million. Our job is to create that income for less. If we can build it for $8 million, all in, our yield on cost is 7.5 percent. The 1.5-point gap over the market rate is our development spread, and it is worth about $2 million of created value. Two things can take it away. Costs can rise, and the cap rate can rise before we finish. So we set a minimum spread before we bid for land, we test cap rates half a point and a point higher, and we only borrow against income the building actually earns. That discipline is why we sometimes walk away from land others buy."

The biggest risk

The biggest risk after a week like this is false fluency: being able to recite the formulas without noticing when an input is wrong. The control is the Red Pen habit. Every time you see a valuation, check what is in NOI, what is in total cost, and which cap rate is being used, before you look at the answer.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner memorises the equations and stops. The professional memorises the traps around them: gross versus net, entry versus exit cap rate, cost with and without land and finance, as-is versus as-stabilised.

Callback

In Week 6 you learned to present numbers aloud: round them, give the unit, and say the one that matters first. Use that in the boardroom drill. "About two million of created value" lands. "One million nine hundred ninety-eight thousand" does not.

Recap

Value equals NOI over cap rate. Yield on cost equals stabilised NOI over total cost. The spread is the difference, and it must pay for the risk. Leverage magnifies cap rate moves. Read appraisals before trusting them. Work backward to the land.

head: The six questions
speak: This week I learned how value is made. A rental building is worth its net operating income divided by the market cap rate. As a developer, I measure yield on cost, stabilised NOI divided by everything it costs to build, and my profit comes from the spread between that and the cap rate. A 7.5 percent yield on cost against a 6 percent cap rate is a 150 basis point spread and about 25 percent profit on cost. Leverage makes cap rate moves hurt more: a one-point rise can take 40 percent of my equity. So I read appraisals carefully, separating as-is from as-stabilised and listing the assumptions. I work backward from the finished building to the most I can pay for land. And I follow Rule 10: I never borrow against income that does not yet exist.
terms: Profit on cost — created value divided by total project cost; equal to yield on cost divided by cap rate, minus one.
Red Pen — Kema's drill of reading a document specifically to find planted or real errors before trusting its conclusion.
False fluency — the ability to recite a method without reliably catching wrong inputs to it.

hostile.q: Your memo says an 8.3 percent yield on cost. Show me what's in the cost.
hostile.a: You are right to ask, because a yield on cost is only as honest as its denominator. My total cost includes land, hard costs, soft costs, contingency and finance costs, including interest during construction. NOI is after vacancy and operating expenses and before debt service, depreciation and tax. I will put the full cost build-up on one page beside the yield, and if any line is missing, the yield is overstated and I will restate it.
